posts.title: Inside the glaze tests: forty shades of one celadon
posts.excerpt: Every spring Sayo Mizunoe hangs forty small tiles on a board in her workshop. Each is the same glaze, fired a little differently. This year one of them changed her mind.
posts.content:
The board hangs by the door of the Mizunoe workshop, where the light is best in the afternoon. Forty small tiles, each with a hole punched at the top, each dipped in what looks like the same milky glaze. Fired, they run from a pale, almost grey sea-glass to a deep pond green.

One recipe, forty kilns

The recipe barely changes. What changes is the thickness of the coat, the position in the kiln and, above all, how much air the fire is allowed. Celadon gets its colour from a trace of iron, and iron turns blue-green only when the kiln is starved of oxygen at the right moment. Too early and the glaze bubbles; too late and it stays yellow.

I make the tiles so I stop arguing with myself. The kiln has the last word anyway.

Sayo Mizunoe

The tile that won

Tile twenty-seven, from the back of the kiln, came out paler than anything Sayo has made before, with a faint blue in the hollows. She liked it enough to fire a whole shelf of rice bowls in that spot. Some of them are in the shop now, and they are the palest celadon we have ever sold.

If you have a Moon Pool bowl from this autumn, turn it over: a small dot in the foot ring marks the tile-twenty-seven batch.

posts.title: Three nights at the wood kiln
posts.excerpt: Ishizuchi Kiln fires twice a year, for four days without a break. We joined the night shift for three of them, and came home smelling of red pine.
posts.content:
The climbing kiln at Ishizuchi runs twenty metres up a cedar slope, five chambers stepped one above the other. Once it is lit, someone must feed it every few minutes, day and night, until the last chamber reaches temperature. Kenji Arata and four friends take shifts. This year, for three nights, we were two of the extra hands.

Feeding the fire

The work is simple and relentless: open the side port, throw in three split logs of red pine, close it, wait, watch the flame through the spy hole. Around two in the morning the kiln roars and the sparks rise like a small festival. By four it is quiet again, and you can hear the pots ticking in the heat.

What the ash does

Wood ash flies through the chambers and settles on the pots, where it melts into glass. On the shoulders of the tall bottles it runs green; on the side facing the fire, the clay flashes orange. Nobody can plan exactly where it will fall. That is why no two Ishizuchi pieces are alike, and why every one in the shop is listed as one of a kind.

The kiln was opened a week later. Three of the bottle vases from that firing are now in the shop, and one is on the shelf in our own kitchen.

posts.title: How we wrap a bowl for a long journey
posts.excerpt: Paper, string, a reused box and about four minutes. Ren learned to wrap paintings for museums; here is how that turned into wrapping bowls.
posts.content:
Before the shop, Ren Okabe spent ten years packing paintings for travelling exhibitions. The rule there was simple: nothing may move, and nothing may touch the surface. It turns out to be a very good rule for bowls too.

Four layers, no plastic

  1. Washi first. A sheet of soft paper around the piece, folded, never taped to the glaze.
  2. Corrugated card. A collar around the widest part, so nothing presses on the rim.
  3. A snug box. Usually one we have saved from a delivery, cut down so the piece cannot shift.
  4. Paper string. Tied once, so you can open it with one pull.

Every parcel also carries a small card with the name of the kiln, the glaze and how to care for the piece. Keep the box if you can: it is the best way to store a bowl you use only for guests.

In nine years we have had eleven breakages in the post. Each was replaced, and most of the broken pieces went to our repairer and came back with gold seams.

posts.title: Golden repair: when a favourite bowl breaks
posts.excerpt: A broken bowl is not the end of it. A note on mending with natural lacquer and gold, and what to do in the first five minutes after it falls.
posts.content:
Sooner or later, a bowl you love will slip. The first thing to do is nothing dramatic: pick up every piece, even the small ones, and put them in a box with a cloth. Do not glue anything. Modern glue makes a later repair much harder.

The slow way

Our repairer in Kanazawa uses the old method: natural lacquer mixed with rice paste to join the pieces, layers of lacquer to fill the gaps, each one left to cure for days in a humid box, and finally a dusting of gold powder along the seam. It takes about two months. Done well, the bowl is food-safe and strong again.

The crack is the bowl's history. We just draw it in gold so nobody forgets.

Our repairer

Caring for a mended piece

Wash by hand in lukewarm water, never in the dishwasher or microwave, and do not leave it to soak. The gold is soft and will wear a little with use, which only makes it look more like part of the bowl.

posts.title: An autumn table with five small dishes
posts.excerpt: Grilled mushrooms, persimmon, a little miso. How five small dishes in five glazes turn an ordinary supper into something that feels like a season.
posts.content:
A Japanese table is less about a big plate in the middle and more about rhythm: lots of small things, each in its own dish, each a little different. It is the easiest way to make a weekday supper feel considered.

Five dishes, five glazes

For an autumn table we use the Dew set from Tsukiyama Kiln: celadon for sliced persimmon, the pale one for pickled turnip, iron-black for grilled shiitake, ash glaze for a spoon of miso, bare clay for roasted chestnuts. Nothing matches; everything belongs.

Add a rice bowl, a soup bowl, chopsticks on a rest, and a single branch in a vase. That is the whole table. It takes five minutes longer to set than one big plate and it changes how slowly everyone eats.

posts.title: Centering: a morning at Tsukiyama Kiln
posts.excerpt: In an old rice store outside Mashiko, Emi and Daichi Kurose make bowls that are a little heavier than most. We spent a morning finding out why.
posts.content:
The Kuroses work in a rice store built in 1931, with thick earth walls that keep the clay cool in summer. Emi throws at the wheel by the window; Daichi trims and glazes at the long table in the back. They have done it this way for twelve years.

Weight on purpose

Their bowls are heavier than the porcelain most people are used to, and that is deliberate. A thicker wall holds heat, sits steady on the table and survives a dishwasher for years. The foot is trimmed round, so the bowl rests in the palm without an edge.

Before a new shape goes to any shop, they use it at their own table for a month. The Iron Rim noodle bowl went through three versions this way: the first was too shallow for broth, the second too heavy to hold in one hand. The third is in the shop.

posts.title: Why celadon crackles, and why we love it
posts.excerpt: That fine net of lines in a celadon glaze is not a flaw. It is the glaze settling, and over years it becomes a map of how you use the piece.
posts.content:
Hold a celadon cup up to the window and you may see it: a fine net of lines under the surface of the glaze. Sometimes it appears weeks after firing, with a tiny ping on a quiet evening. People often write to us worried that something has cracked. It has not.

Glass on stone

A glaze is a thin layer of glass fused to clay. As the piece cools, the glass shrinks a little more than the clay beneath it, and the tension is released as crackle. The lines live only in the glaze; the body underneath is whole and watertight.

Over time, tea and food colour the lines, and a cup used every morning slowly darkens into a pattern of its own. If you would rather keep it pale, rinse soon after use and let it dry fully. If you love the map, as we do, simply keep using it.

products.name: Moon Pool Rice Bowl
products.short: Our best-loved rice bowl: celadon that pools deep teal in the well, with a bare clay foot ring. Mizunoe Kiln.
products.description:
Sayo Mizunoe glazes this bowl thick, so the celadon gathers in the bottom like a small moon reflected in water. The rim is thin and slightly flared, the foot left bare so you can feel the grey stoneware underneath.

Each bowl is thrown by hand, so sizes and the depth of colour vary a little. The one you receive will be wrapped in paper and sent with a care card.

products.name: Still Water Plate, 24 cm
products.short: A wide dinner plate with a glassy pool of celadon in the centre and a fine crackle that deepens with use.
products.description: A broad, low plate with a gently raised rim, made for a main course or a shared dish in the middle of the table. The glaze settles into a clear pool in the centre and crackles finely as it cools, a pattern that slowly darkens over the years.

products.name: Ripple Teacup
products.short: A tall porcelain teacup carved with fine ripples under a pale seiji glaze. Light, thin and warm in the hand.
products.description: Haru Odagiri carves each cup by hand with a bent wire, so the ripples run slightly uneven, like water after a stone. The pale seiji glaze fills the grooves and leaves the ridges almost white.

products.name: Ash Glaze Bottle Vase
products.short: A tall bottle vase from the wood kiln, with green ash glaze running from the shoulder. One of a kind.
products.description:
This bottle stood near the firebox for four days, where the ash fell thickest. It melted on the shoulder and ran down in green rivulets, stopping just above the foot. The clay shows warm orange where the flame touched it.

A single stem or a branch of autumn leaves is all it needs.

products.name: River Stone Sake Set
products.short: A sake flask and two cups, dipped halfway in pale celadon so the bare stoneware shows below. Boxed for giving.
products.description: Kenji Arata holds each piece by the foot and dips it once, so the line where the glaze stops is a little different every time. Warm or cold sake both suit it; so does barley tea in summer.

details.Glaze: Pale celadon dip over bare stoneware

products.name: Dew Small Dishes, set of five
products.short: Five small dishes in five glazes, for pickles, soy sauce, a sweet or a single bite of something good.
products.description: Small dishes are where a Japanese table gets its rhythm. This set gathers five of the Kuroses' glazes in one stack, so you can mix them freely, and the set grows nicely if you add a second.

details.Glaze: Five glazes: celadon, pale, iron black, ash and bare clay

products.name: Iron Rim Noodle Bowl
products.short: A generous bowl for noodles, soup or salad: celadon inside, an iron-black rim, and a foot that sits well in the hand.
products.description: Wide enough for a full bowl of udon with everything on top, deep enough to keep the broth hot. The iron rim is brushed on by hand and fires almost black, a quiet frame for whatever you put inside.

products.name: Tide Oval Platter
products.short: A long oval platter for fish or a shared dish, with a carved centre where the celadon pools like a tide line.
products.description: Made by pressing a slab over a hand-carved mould, then trimming the rim by eye. The carving in the middle catches the glaze in shallow waves, so the platter looks different from every side of the table.

products.name: Pebble Chopstick Rests, set of four
products.short: Four porcelain chopstick rests shaped like river pebbles, each in a different glaze. A small, perfect gift.
products.description: Haru Odagiri makes these from the trimmings of larger pieces, pressing each one between her palms. They are small enough to post in a letter, though we always send them in a box.

products.name: Carved Celadon Lidded Jar
products.short: A round porcelain jar carved with petals, under a pale celadon that pools in every cut. For tea, sugar or nothing at all.
products.description: Thirty-two petals, each cut in a single stroke. The lid is thrown from the same clay and fired in place on the jar, so it fits only this one. It is the most time-consuming thing we sell, and Haru makes only a few each season.
